Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Cuba, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), which rejected her refugee protection claim.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Cuba, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), which rejected her refugee protection claim.
The appellant is not presenting any new evidence in support of her appeal, nor is she asking that a hearing be held before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

Under subsection 111(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the RPD's determination, namely, that the appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.
The appeal is dismissed.
Reportedly, the appellant always had anti-government opinions and did not want to participate in political activities in Cuba or join the communist party.
However, she was allegedly a member of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and the Cuban Women's Federation.

The appellant supposedly studied to be a XXXX XXXX. Apparently, she did not find any work in this field because she did not have a youth booklet. Consequently, the appellant allegedly studied XXXX and joined the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in 2007 as a XXXX XXXX.
This XXXX had a XXXX XXXX, the XXXX XXXX, which was reportedly XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012 because the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXthe national average (see RPD record, page 71).
However, the appellant and XXXX XXXX allegedly continued to XXXX after this date [translation] "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX" (see RPD record, page 72).
It is in this context that the appellant and other members of her XXXX supposedly obtained a work visa for Canada in XXXX 2014 to come here and XXXX on stage.
The appellant left Cuba in XXXX 2014 and claimed refugee protection on November 3, 2014.

The RPD concluded that the appellant, although credible with regard to her job as a XXXX XXXX XXXX member for the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, as well as her unwillingness to participate in government activities, failed to establish that she would face a reasonable chance of persecution or of being subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to her life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she returned to Cuba.

This is because the appellant did not establish that she had been mistreated in Cuba before she left. The RPD noted in particular that the appellant was unable to explain how she had been harassed in Cuba and that, when she explained how she had been controlled by the CDR, she stated that she was simply asked questions.

Furthermore, the RPD was of the opinion that the appellant did not establish that she had been unable to find work since the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, considering that attending XXXX XXXX XXXX since XXXX XXXX XXXX and not trying to find a job in line with her XXXX XXXX training did not satisfy the [translation] "element of repetition and relentlessness found at the heart of persecution."
The appellant's grounds of appeal can be summarized as follows:
The RPD erred by titling one of its sections [translation] "Credibility" even though its analysis does not make any reference to credibility.

The RPD misassessed the evidence by failing to consider that it was because of the expression of her political opinion, either through her refusal to participate in the government's propaganda activities or her refusal to be a member of the communist party, or in the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, that the appellant was unable to find employment since XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The appellant is of the opinion that the RPD misassessed the evidence by not concluding that this was persecution.

The RAD is a newly constituted appeal tribunal for RPD decisions whose role has not yet been clarified. The IRPA does not expressly set out the standard of review and intervention to be applied to appeals of RPD decisions.

To date, Federal Court decisions have established that the RAD is a "specialized (if not overspecialized) tribunal" (see Alvarez)1 and that Parliament conferred "a true appellate function on the RAD...which sits on appeal of the decisions of another administrative tribunal." The RAD "also has the authority to investigate, an authority the Federal Court judge...does not have."

The Honourable Justice Shore in Alvarez2 is of the opinion that "Parliament seems to have wanted to confer a broad power of intervention on the RAD, thus allowing the RAD to dispose of the merits of appeals and not only to determine whether the RPD's decision was made in a reasonable manner...." These appeals are not appeals de novo, and the RAD can hold a hearing only where new evidence is presented in accordance with subsections 110(3), 110(4) and 110(6) of the IRPA; this limits the scope of the appeal that the IRPA confers on the RAD. The appeal is also not a judicial review whose sole purpose is to determine whether the RPD's decision was reasonable.

In Eng,3 Justice Shore is of the view that although the RPD, as the tribunal of first instance, is owed deference by the RAD with regard to findings of fact, as it is better situated, having seen and heard the claimant, the RAD must nonetheless perform its own assessment of all the evidence. This is done "in order to determine whether the RPD relied on a wrong principle of law or misassessed the facts to the point of making a palpable and overriding error" (Eng).4

In Huruglica, Justice Phelan states, "In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion...."

Thus, Huruglica advocates an approach where deference must be shown to the RPD with respect to the assessment of credibility while conducting an independent analysis of credibility without being restricted to "a palpable and overriding error." Regarding the analysis of the documentary evidence, the Honourable Justice Phelan is of the opinion that the RAD has expertise that is equal to or greater than that of the RPD "in the interpretation of country condition evidence. Unlike a court and the supervisory nature of judicial oversight, there is no reason for the RAD to defer to the RPD on this type of assessment."5

The Honourable Justice Roy in Spasoja, subsequent to Huruglica, expresses a different opinion than that of the Honourable Justice Phelan in Huruglica. In his view, the standard of review before the RAD must be "palpable and overriding error" on questions of fact; the RAD must show deference to the RPD's credibility findings; and on questions of law, the appropriate standard is correctness. This conclusion is consistent with the decisions in Alvarez and Eng.

In Alyafi6 Justice Martineau's view is that both positions, the first set out in Alvarez, Eng and Spasoja (palpable and overriding error) and the second in Huruglica (described by Justice Martineau as "a composite and variable standard of review resulting from the nature of the claim before the RAD-characterized as a 'hybrid appeal'") (Alyafi, para. 16), may both be applied as long as the scope of the appeal has not been settled definitively by a ruling of the Federal Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada.

It seems to me that the RAD must show a measure of deference to the RPD's credibility findings in accordance with the Huruglica decision, considering that the RPD had the opportunity to see, question and hear the appellant.

The RAD will conduct its own analysis and consider all the evidence, including the appellant's testimony, and it will conduct its own analysis while showing a measure of deference to the RPD with respect to credibility issues.

The RAD will intervene only where it is of the opinion that the RPD's findings on questions of fact or of mixed fact and law are erroneous or are not supported by the evidence, in accordance with subsections 111(1) and 111(2) of the IRPA. With respect to errors of law, the standard of review that the RAD will apply is correctness (Spasoja).7 ANALYSIS
The RAD reviewed the record as a whole, particularly the recording of the hearing before the RPD. It is of the opinion that the RPD rendered the correct decision.
The appellant states that the RPD erred by titling a section "Credibility" even though it does not deal with credibility.

Although this may be confusing, it is clear, however, when reading the paragraph that follows this title, that the decision is based on two factors: - The first is to the effect that the appellant is credible with regard to her role as a choir member and that she did not want to participate in government propaganda activities. - The second factor involves the fear of persecution.
The RAD does not see any intention to mislead the reader and is of the opinion that, when read, the decision is not confusing.

To establish the existence of a serious possibility of persecution, the appellant must establish that she has a subjective and objective fear. In this case, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant did not establish the existence of an objective fear of persecution. She did not establish that she would face more than a mere possibility of being persecuted if she returned.
The appellant testified that she was considered counter-revolutionary in her country because of her refusal to participate in political pro-government demonstrations and join the communist party.

The appellant allegedly pursued higher education as a XXXX XXXX. The appellant stated that one had to be a member of the communist party to be admitted to this institution. The appellant was not, but she was allegedly still admitted and succeeded in obtaining her diploma.
Consequently, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant was not perceived by the state as being counter-revolutionary. Otherwise, she would not have been admitted and obtained a diploma.
The appellant testified that the events she experienced in Cuba, besides the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and the alleged problems finding a job afterwards, are as follows:

She was questioned by the president of the CDR, who asked her why she did not participate more in politics, and she was stopped by officers of the state while she was in the company of tourists. They told her to leave and that she could be fined. However, there were no consequences.
This does not constitute persecution, neither cumulatively nor on its own.

Despite the restrictions that applied in Cuba until late 2012 (since January 14, 2013, it is no longer necessary to obtain an exit permit to leave Cuba, see RPD record, page 50, response from the IRB documentation centre, Tab 4.3), the appellant was able to obtain an exit permit for a period of 75 days and had her passport extended (see RPD record, page 94).

The documentation states that persons who are perceived as government opponents are seen in a negative light by the government, which controls all spheres of public life, and are subjected to repression. Many of them were prevented from leaving Cuba, both before and after the application of new travel rules (see RPD record, page 36, Tab 2.2).

The appellant was able to obtain a passport and an exit permit, she was able to pursue higher education at a school where only members of the communist party were admitted, and she was able to study XXXX, work with XXXX XXXX and take a trip abroad XXXX XXXX.
The RAD is of the opinion that if the appellant had truly been perceived as opposing the government, she would not objectively have been able to obtain these privileges.
The appellant argues in her memorandum that the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was an act of repression by the government against this centre because the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
There is nothing in the evidence that the appellant cites in her memorandum on page 6 (see RPD record, pages 69 to 74) that suggests that such is the case. The RAD did not read this.

Rather, it indicates that XXXX XXXX XXXX following state intervention because this XXXX XXXX was opened at a time of openness toward small businesses by Raoul Castro. The director took advantage of this to make some developments and allegedly built a XXXX in addition to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX

The government allegedly XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012, accusing those in charge of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The employees were XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX while the average was XXXX XXXX, which the Cuban government did not like.
Furthermore, there is nothing in this document that indicates that, afterwards, this XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. This is not suggested in the information from the evidence cited by the appellant.

Rather, the evidence indicates that this XXXX XXXX XXXX work afterwards, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX across Cuba, in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Furthermore, according to this document, the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXe had to perform abroad.
This information is consistent with the fact that the appellant was able to obtain an exit visa for a period of 75 days in order to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in Canada with XXXX XXXX.
In light of the evidence on the record, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant did not establish that she was unable to work after XXXX XXXX XXXX.
In the circumstances, the RAD is of the opinion that she did not establish the existence of an objective fear of persecution.

The RAD is of the opinion that the appellant failed to establish under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA that there are serious reasons to believe that she would be persecuted because of her political opinion or that she would be subjected to a risk to her life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment under section 97 of the IRPA, or to a danger of torture.
The RPD rendered the correct decision and did not err.

For these reasons, the RAD confirms the RPD's determination, namely, that XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed. Roxane Cyr Roxane Cyr September 8, 2015 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 Alvarez v.
